extraction_metadata.notes: Harvard Medical School researchers developed G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR)-based fluorescent sensors that light up when specific neuromodulators bind to their extracellular surface. A direct experimental readout of GPCR conformational state — bridging the cellular-signaling and GPCR conformational landscape concept cards.

title: GPCR-based fluorescent sensors light up when neuromodulators bind
subtitle_or_tagline: Harvard Medical School turns the receptor's conformational change itself into an optical readout
topic: Harvard Medical School researchers engineered G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR)-based fluorescent sensors that fluoresce when particular neuromodulators bind to them on the cell surface. Rather than measuring downstream second messengers (cAMP, calcium), the sensor couples the receptor's own conformational change to a fluorophore — turning the receptor into a real-time optical reporter of its own activation state. This enables spatially and temporally resolved maps of neuromodulator signaling in living tissue.

components.name: GPCR Scaffold
components.role: Natural receptor providing ligand specificity and conformational change

components.name: Fluorophore Module
components.role: Insertion point whose fluorescence is gated by receptor conformation

components.name: Optical Readout
components.role: Real-time fluorescence reporting in living cells and tissue

architecture.data_flow: neuromodulator binds -> GPCR conformational shift -> fluorophore environment changes -> fluorescence signal

workflow_steps: Step 1 - Engineer GPCR scaffold with conformationally-gated fluorophore
Step 2 - Validate sensor specificity for target neuromodulator
Step 3 - Express sensor in living cells or tissue
Step 4 - Image fluorescence changes in real time as neuromodulators bind
Step 5 - Map spatial and temporal patterns of signaling activity
key_claims: Sensors light up when specific neuromodulators bind to the receptor surface
Readout is the receptor's own conformational change, not a downstream proxy
Enables real-time imaging of neuromodulator signaling in living systems
GPCR family provides a modular scaffold for multiple neuromodulator targets
Developed by Harvard Medical School researchers (highlighted in HMS post)
caveats_or_warnings: Fluorophore insertion can perturb native receptor kinetics
Signal calibration varies per receptor-ligand pair
Expression levels must be controlled to avoid saturating the readout
osiris_connection: The fluorescent sensor makes GPCR conformational state directly observable — it is an experimental instrument for the exact quantity the gpcr-conformational-landscape card models. In OSIRIS terms, the sensor is a bound-certifying readout: fluorescence intensity is a monotonic function of conformational displacement, so the optical signal provides an empirical upper bound on how far the receptor has moved from its inactive state. The signaling-cascade theorem (cumulative displacement bounded by L*c through the cascade) acquires here a direct experimental measurement channel: each receptor's conformational displacement becomes visible, layer by layer, in living tissue.
